note: GLOBALCIT's Citizenship Law Dataset v3.0 (EUI, 2025), coding the law in force on 1 January 2024 (A06a Const 30B(1, 2), MEX 19-21, 25, REG 15; A06b Const 30B(1, 2), MEX 19-21, 25, REG 15; L05 Const 37B(1)): ordinary naturalisation after 5 years' residence; the applicant must give up other citizenships; a citizen keeps it on taking another (loss applies only to naturalised citizens, not modelled). Reforms after that date are checked in the file's later sources, where a later source is given. Citizenship at birth is read from the same dataset's 2024 coding of modes A01a (descent, born in country: No provision), A01b (descent, born abroad: Generational transmission restriction: conditional on birthplace/place of residence /mode under which parent acquired citizenship), A02a (birth in country: Generally applicable provision) and A02b (birth in country to a parent born there: No provision), as its codebook (RSC/GLOBALCIT 2025/01, sections 3.2.1a to 3.2.2b) defines them: by birth in the territory unconditionally; by descent from either parent, a child born abroad on the limit the dataset states (the dataset codes no separate descent rule for a child born in the country, birth there giving it; the parent's sex is read from mode A01b). Changes to the law at birth after 1 January 2024 weren't checked for this file. A naturalisation letter costs MX$9,502.01 in duties (Federal Duties Law art. 26(II), as the Chamber of Deputies publishes it with amounts updated by the Miscellaneous Tax Resolution of 28 December 2025); the applicant must prove speaking Spanish, knowing the country's history and integration into the national culture (Nationality Law art. 19(III), last reformed 23 April 2012). The Foreign Ministry's own pages refused this research's requests behind a browser check, so no time is held.
